feature.title: The Beagle voyage, 1831 to 1836
feature.lead: A survey ship went round the world, and a 22-year-old naturalist went with it. Follow the stops where Darwin collected the facts he would think about for the rest of his life.

items.label: Plymouth
items.text: After several false starts, HMS Beagle sailed under Captain Robert FitzRoy to survey the coasts of South America. Darwin went as an unpaid gentleman companion and naturalist.

items.label: Tenerife
items.place: Santa Cruz de Tenerife, Canary Islands, (Spain)
items.text: Darwin had dreamed of exploring Tenerife, but the ship was put in quarantine because of cholera in England. No one could land, and the Beagle sailed on.

items.label: Cape Verde
items.text: His first tropical landfall. Over about 23 days he studied the rocks of Quail Island, collected sea animals and explored valleys inland.

items.label: St Paul's Rocks
items.place: St Peter and St Paul Archipelago, (Brazil)
items.text: A tiny group of bare rocks in the open Atlantic. Darwin landed with FitzRoy and collected the seabirds, which were so tame they did not fly away. The ship crossed the equator the next day.

items.label: Bahia
items.text: Darwin walked in a tropical rainforest for the first time and was amazed. He was also appalled by slavery, and argued about it with FitzRoy.

items.label: Rio de Janeiro
items.text: He stayed in a cottage at Botafogo and rode inland to the Macae River, collecting insects, plants and animals while the ship surveyed the coast.

items.label: Punta Alta
items.text: In low cliffs Darwin dug out bones of huge extinct mammals, including parts of giant ground sloths. Why had these giants vanished, and why did they resemble living animals nearby?

items.label: Tierra del Fuego
items.text: The Beagle returned three Fuegians whom FitzRoy had taken to England on an earlier voyage. A small mission was set up for them, but it soon failed.

items.label: Falkland Islands
items.text: Darwin studied the plants and animals and found fossils. He also hired Syms Covington, a crew member, as his full-time servant and helper with the collections.

items.label: Santa Cruz River
items.text: Darwin joined an expedition up the river. He studied the step-like terraces of land and discussed with FitzRoy how they had formed.

items.label: Valparaiso
items.text: He climbed Cerro La Campana and travelled inland, then fell seriously ill in September. Some writers think he caught a disease here, but that is disputed.

items.label: Valdivia earthquake
items.text: Darwin was ashore for a great earthquake. At Concepcion two weeks later he saw the ruined town, and FitzRoy measured that the land had risen by about 9 feet. The earth was still moving.

items.label: The Andes
items.text: High in the mountains, at about 13,000 feet, he found fossil seashells. Rock that had once been seabed was now on top of the world.

items.label: Galapagos Islands
items.text: For five weeks Darwin collected on Chatham, Charles, Albemarle and James islands. He noticed the mockingbirds differed between islands. Only back in England did experts show how many new species he had found.

items.label: Tahiti
items.text: After 25 days at sea from the Galapagos, Darwin admired the island's plants and found the islanders intelligent.

items.label: New Zealand
items.text: Darwin was critical of conditions there and of some of the English settlers, and was glad to leave on 30 December.

items.label: Australia
items.text: In Australia he met Aboriginal people, examined a platypus and caught a potoroo. In Tasmania he wrote critically of how settlers had treated the Aboriginal people.

items.label: Cocos (Keeling)
items.text: The crew surveyed a coral atoll to test Darwin's idea that reefs grow upward as the land beneath them slowly sinks. It became his first big scientific theory.

items.label: Cape Town
items.text: Darwin learned that Henslow had printed his letters, so he was already known to scientists at home. Around 15 June he met the astronomer John Herschel.

items.label: Falmouth
items.text: After stops at St Helena, Ascension, Brazil and the Azores, the Beagle anchored in Falmouth. Darwin reached his family at Shrewsbury two days later.

timeline.title: Born at The Mount
timeline.text: Charles Robert Darwin was born at the family home, The Mount, in Shrewsbury. His father Robert was a doctor. His grandfathers were the thinker Erasmus Darwin and the potter Josiah Wedgwood.

timeline.title: His mother dies
timeline.text: His mother Susannah died when he was eight. That year he had started at a local day school. In 1818 he went to board at Shrewsbury School with his older brother Erasmus.

timeline.title: Medical school in Edinburgh
timeline.text: He went to study medicine at the University of Edinburgh. He found the lectures dull and neglected his studies. Instead he joined the Plinian Society, a student natural history club.

timeline.title: A first discovery
timeline.text: At the student Plinian Society he reported that small black spores found in oyster shells were in fact the eggs of a leech. It was his first scientific finding.

timeline.title: Cambridge and the beetles
timeline.text: His father sent him to Christ's College, Cambridge, to train as a clergyman. He wrote that nothing there gave him as much pleasure as collecting beetles. He became a close follower of the botany professor John Stevens Henslow.

timeline.title: Field trip with Sedgwick
timeline.text: After passing his degree exam in January, tenth of 178, he spent about two weeks with the geologist Adam Sedgwick mapping rock layers in Wales.

timeline.title: The letter from Henslow
timeline.text: He came home to find a letter from Henslow proposing him for an unpaid place on HMS Beagle, as a companion to Captain FitzRoy. He was not the first choice. His father objected at first, but agreed when Darwin's uncle Josiah Wedgwood argued for the trip.

timeline.title: The Beagle sails
timeline.text: HMS Beagle left Plymouth on a survey voyage planned for two years. It lasted almost five. Darwin was badly seasick early on and spent much of the voyage exploring on land.

timeline.title: Rainforest and slavery
timeline.text: In Brazil he walked in the tropical forest for the first time. He was appalled by slavery and quarrelled with FitzRoy about it. FitzRoy later apologised.

timeline.title: Giant fossils
timeline.text: At Punta Alta he dug out the bones of huge extinct mammals. He shipped fossils home to Henslow, who praised the collections.

timeline.title: Tierra del Fuego
timeline.text: The Beagle brought three Fuegians home after a stay in England. Darwin compared them with the local Yaghan people. The mission set up for them soon failed.

timeline.title: The earthquake
timeline.text: Darwin was ashore at Valdivia during a severe earthquake. At Concepcion he saw that the land had risen by about 9 feet, proof that the earth's surface still moves.

timeline.title: Seashells in the Andes
timeline.text: Crossing the Andes, he reached the high divide at about 13,000 feet and found fossil seashells. Old seabed had been lifted into mountains.

timeline.title: The Galapagos
timeline.text: For five weeks he collected on four islands. He labelled his mockingbirds by island but not his finches. Only later did he learn that tortoises and birds varied from island to island, a clue to how species form.

timeline.title: Home again
timeline.text: The Beagle anchored at Falmouth after almost five years. Because Henslow had shared his letters, Darwin came home already known to scientists. On 29 October he met the geologist Charles Lyell.

timeline.title: Gould's surprise
timeline.text: The bird expert John Gould reported that Darwin's Galapagos 'blackbirds', 'grosbeaks' and 'finches' were a new group of 12 species of ground finch. By March he found the mockingbirds were separate species too.

timeline.title: "I think"
timeline.text: He began a private notebook on how species might change. On page 36 he drew his first tree of life and wrote 'I think' above it.

timeline.title: Reading Malthus
timeline.text: He read Thomas Malthus's essay on population. It showed him how competition could keep helpful variations and remove harmful ones: natural selection. His notes date this to 28 September; his later Autobiography says October.

timeline.title: Marries Emma Wedgwood
timeline.text: Five days after being elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, he married his cousin Emma Wedgwood. He had shared his ideas with her when he proposed.

timeline.title: The Beagle journal
timeline.text: His journal of the voyage was published as the third volume of FitzRoy's account. Today it is known as The Voyage of the Beagle and made his name with the public.

timeline.title: Down House
timeline.text: The family moved to Down House in the Kent countryside, where he lived and worked for about 40 years. That year he also published his book on coral reefs and wrote a short pencil sketch of his theory.

timeline.title: The 1844 essay
timeline.text: He expanded his sketch into a 230-page essay, but did not publish it. In January he had told the botanist Joseph Hooker about his theory in confidence.

timeline.title: Eight years of barnacles
timeline.text: He began a close study of barnacles that lasted until 1854. In 1853 the Royal Society gave him its Royal Medal.

timeline.title: Annie dies
timeline.text: His ten-year-old daughter Annie died while he had taken her for treatment at Malvern. Charles and Emma kept a box of her keepsakes for the rest of their lives.

timeline.title: Wallace's letter
timeline.text: A paper arrived from the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace, working in the Malay Archipelago, with the same idea of natural selection. As Wallace asked, Darwin sent it on to Lyell that day.

timeline.title: A joint announcement
timeline.text: Lyell and Hooker presented Wallace's paper and extracts of Darwin's work together at the Linnean Society. Darwin was not there: his baby son Charles had died three days before.

timeline.title: On the Origin of Species
timeline.text: John Murray published the book at 15 shillings. The first printing of 1,250 copies sold out to booksellers. It set out the evidence that species change over time by natural selection.

timeline.title: The Oxford debate
timeline.text: At a British Association meeting in Oxford, supporters and critics argued about his theory in a famous debate. Scientists, philosophers and clergy argued about the book for years.

timeline.title: The Copley Medal
timeline.text: The Royal Society awarded him the Copley Medal, its highest honour. He kept working at Down House on plants, studying orchids, climbing plants and how flowers are pollinated.

timeline.title: The Descent of Man
timeline.text: He applied his theory to human beings in The Descent of Man, and followed it in 1872 with a book on how people and animals express emotions.

timeline.title: The book on worms
timeline.text: His last book showed how earthworms slowly turn and build the soil. He had first spoken about worms and soil in 1837, more than 40 years before.

timeline.title: Death at Down House
timeline.text: Darwin died at Down House at 73, after heart trouble in his last months.

timeline.title: Burial in Westminster Abbey
timeline.text: After a funeral on 26 April he was buried in Westminster Abbey, next to the astronomer John Herschel and near Isaac Newton.

timeline.title: The Darwin-Wallace Medal
timeline.text: The Linnean Society first awarded the Darwin-Wallace Medal, honouring both men who announced natural selection together.

timeline.title: On the ten-pound note
timeline.text: His portrait appeared on the Bank of England ten-pound note from 2000 to 2017. His letters and works are now free to read online through Cambridge University and Darwin Online.

works.title: Journal of Researches (The Voyage of the Beagle)
works.text: His lively account of the five-year voyage, revised in 1845. It made him famous as a travel writer and naturalist.

works.title: Zoology of the Voyage of H.M.S. Beagle
works.text: Five parts published from 1838 to 1843, edited by Darwin, describing the animals he collected, written with experts such as John Gould.

works.title: The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs
works.text: His theory that reefs and atolls grow as the land beneath them slowly sinks, worked out on the voyage.

works.title: Geological Observations on the Volcanic Islands
works.text: The second of his three geology books from the voyage.

works.title: Geological Observations on South America
works.text: His study of the rising land, fossils and mountains of South America.

works.title: Barnacle monographs
works.text: Detailed studies of living and fossil barnacles, published from 1851 to 1854. Eight years of careful work on one group of animals.

works.title: Joint papers with Wallace
works.text: Extracts from his unpublished work, read at the Linnean Society with Alfred Russel Wallace's paper on the same idea.

works.title: On the Origin of Species
works.text: The book that set out evolution by natural selection, with years of evidence. Six editions appeared in his lifetime.

works.title: Fertilisation of Orchids
works.text: How the shapes of orchid flowers help insects carry their pollen.

works.title: The Movements and Habits of Climbing Plants
works.text: A study of how climbing plants twist and reach, first a Linnean Society paper and then a book in 1875.

works.title: The Variation of Animals and Plants Under Domestication
works.text: A large collection of evidence from farm animals, pets and crops on how living things vary.

works.title: The Descent of Man
works.text: His theory applied to human beings, together with his idea of sexual selection.

works.title: The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals
works.text: How people and animals show feelings in their faces and bodies.

works.title: Insectivorous Plants
works.text: Experiments on sundews and other plants that catch insects.

works.title: The Power of Movement in Plants
works.text: Experiments on how plant shoots bend towards light.

works.title: The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms
works.text: His last book, on how earthworms build and turn the soil.
